- [00:17](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=17s) The problem is about finding the minimum capacity needed to ship packages within a given number of days.
- [01:49](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=1m49s) An example is given where if the ship's capacity is 100, all packages can be shipped in one day.
- [03:22](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=3m22s) It is demonstrated that a capacity of 10 leads to shipping taking more than the given number of days.
- [04:20](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=4m20s) Increasing the capacity to 15 allows shipping all packages within the given days.
- [06:11](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=6m11s) The answer must be between the maximum weight of a product and the sum of all weights.
- [08:01](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=8m1s) A function is described to find the number of days required to ship with a given capacity.
- [12:32](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=12m32s) The initial solution has a time complexity of O(N^2) due to linear search.
- [13:54](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=13m54s) Binary search is introduced as an optimization technique to find the minimum capacity needed.
- [16:49](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=16m49s) The binary search approach eliminates capacities that are not possible and updates the answer with the lowest possible capacity.
- [18:25](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=18m25s) The time complexity of the binary search solution is O(N * log(Sum - Max)), where N is the number of items and Sum and Max are the sum of weights and the maximum weight, respectively.
- [19:50](https://youtu.be/Mde2q7GFCrw?t=19m50s) The C++ code for the binary search solution is demonstrated, and viewers are encouraged to find code for other programming languages in the video description.

instead of using a while loop to trim down the window, we can rather save the index of the odd elements. This will help us to directly jump the left pointer to that index instead of iterating to that index.
I did it on my own using a queue and sliding window.

Here's the code for the same:


int numberOflessSubarrays(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
queue<int> q;
int left = 0;
int right = 0;
int count = 0;
int answer=0;
while(right<nums.size()){
if(nums[right]%2){
q.push(right);
count++;
}
if(count>k){
left = q.front()+1;
q.pop();
count--;
}
if(count<=k){
answer+=(right-left+1);
}
right++;

}
return answer;
}
int numberOfSubarrays(vector<int>& nums, int k){
return numberOflessSubarrays(nums,k) - numberOflessSubarrays(nums,k-1);
}

Anyone wondering how this is a greedy problem or why we need to prioritize 10+5 in return for 20 over 3 fives, it is because a smart vendor always saves smaller denominations as they are more versatile and used more often for change. Consider the scenario where you have:
5 = 3, 10 = 1
Now when a customer comes with a 20$ bill, let's say you return 3 fives, but now when a customer comes with a 10 dollar bill you can't sell to them, instead if you gave a 10 and a 5 bill to the previous customer, you could sell it to two customers with 10 dollar bills consecutively. Hence it is a greedy approach and we are trying to save 5 dollar bills so that we can serve more customers.

void dfs(Node* root, vector<Node*> &inorder){
if(root == NULL) return;
dfs(root->left, inorder);
inorder.push_back(root);
dfs(root->right, inorder);
}

void correctBST( struct Node* root )
{
vector<Node*> inorder;
dfs(root, inorder);
int ct = 0;
vector<int> pos;
for(int i = 1; i < inorder.size(); i++){
if(inorder[i]->data < inorder[i-1]->data){
pos.push_back(i);
ct++;
}
}
if(ct == 1){
swap(inorder[pos[0] - 1]->data, inorder[pos[0]]->data);
}
else if(ct == 2){
swap(inorder[pos[0]-1]->data, inorder[pos[1]]->data);
}
}

public static int findCelebrity(int n) {
Stack<Integer> stk = new Stack<>();
for(int i=0; i<n; i++) {
stk.push(i);
}

while(stk.size() > 1) {
int a = stk.pop();
int b = stk.pop();

if(Runner.knows(a, b)) {
stk.push(b);
} else {
stk.push(a);
}
}

int candidate = stk.pop();

// Verify candidate
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
if(i != candidate) { // same person
if(Runner.knows(candidate, i) || !Runner.knows(i, candidate)) {
return -1; // No celebrity
}
}
}

return candidate;
}

def maxProfit(self, prices: List[int]) -> int:

min_elem = prices[0]
max_profit = 0

if len(prices) == 1:
return 0
else:
for index,item in enumerate(prices):
if index > 0:
diff = item - min_elem
if diff < 0:
min_elem = item
continue
else:
max_profit = max(max_profit,diff)

class Solution {
public:
bool search(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
auto it = unique(nums.begin(), nums.end());
nums.erase(it, nums.end()); // Erase the duplicates
int n = nums.size();
int low = 0;
int high = n-1;
while(low <= high) {
int mid = low+(high-low)/2;
if(nums[mid] == target) return true;
if(nums[low] <= nums[mid]) {
if(nums[low] <= target && target <= nums[mid]) {
high = mid-1;
}
else low = mid+1;
}
else {
if(nums[mid] <= target && target <= nums[high]) {
low = mid+1;
}
else high = mid-1;
}
}
return false;
}
};

text_display:
Small correction -
you need to do
long n = abs((long) dividend);
long d = abs((long) divisor);
Because if not then we are doing abs of int dividend and in case the dividend is -2^31 it will overflow;

We can start our cnt from 32 (declared outside) and that way we won't have to increment it uptill 32, 31, 30... in order to find the point where ((d << cnt) > n) each time as the outer while loop iterates.
This way we can simply keep decrementing cnt it until 0. Time complexity: O(32) which is as good as constant.

class Solution {
public int divide(int dividend, int divisor) {
if(dividend == divisor) return 1;
boolean sign = true;
if(dividend<0 && divisor>0) sign = false;
if(dividend>0 && divisor<0) sign = false;
long n = Math.abs((long)dividend);
long d = Math.abs((long)divisor);
long ans = 0;
while(n>=d){
int count = 0;
while(n>=(d<<(count+1))) count = count + 1;
ans = ans + (1<<count);
n = n - (d<<count);
}
if(ans==(1<<31) && sign == true) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
if(ans==(1<<31) && sign == false) return Integer.MIN_VALUE;
return sign?(int)ans:(int)-ans;
}
}

This one works with 32 bit integers and is similar to Strivers solution:

class Solution {
public:
int divide(int dividend, int divisor) {
if(dividend == divisor)
return 1;
if (dividend == INT_MIN && divisor == -1) return INT_MAX;
int sign = 1;

if(dividend>=0 and divisor<0) sign =-1;
else if(dividend<=0 and divisor>0) sign=-1;

uint n=abs(dividend);
uint d=abs(divisor);
uint quotient=0;
while(n>=d){
int cnt=0;
while(n>d<<(cnt+1)){
++cnt;
}
quotient += 1<<cnt;
n = n - (d<<cnt);
}
if(quotient== (1<<31) and sign==1){
return INT_MAX;
}
if(quotient== (1<<31) and sign==-1){
return INT_MIN;
}

return sign*quotient;
}
};

int maxMeetings(vector<int>& start, vector<int>& end) {
int n = start.size();
vector<pair<int, int>> meetings;

// Step 1: Pair each meeting's end time with its start time
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
meetings.push_back({end[i], start[i]});
}

// Step 2: Sort meetings by end time (greedy strategy)
sort(meetings.begin(), meetings.end());

// Step 3: Always select the first meeting
int count = 1;
int lastEnd = meetings[0].first; // end time of first meeting

// Step 4: Iterate through the rest of the meetings
for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
// If the current meeting starts after the last selected one ends
if (meetings[i].second > lastEnd) {
count++; // select this meeting
lastEnd = meetings[i].first; // update last end time
}
}

return count; // total number of non-overlapping meetings
}
};

// brute force using map
// optimised using bit manipulation bucket
// approach : we know that all duos xor will be 0 and the unique 2 elements xor will contain

// now we need to distinguish both the numbers
// and xor contains all the bits which are not same in both , we just need one different bit
// taking the rightmost one is fine
long long rightBit= numXor ^ (numXor &(numXor-1));
// now take 2 bucket integer which store numbers based on this rightBit
int a=0,b=0;
for(auto it:nums){
// if right bit is set
if(it&rightBit)a^=it;
else b^=it;
}
return {a,b};
}

Example: Counting people by weight categories
Imagine you have a group of people, and each person has a specific weight. You want to know how many people weigh exactly 70 kg.

Step 1: Count all people weighing less than or equal to 70 kg
This will include people who weigh:

Less than 70 kg (like 60 kg, 50 kg, etc.)
Exactly 70 kg
Let’s say we count all the people who weigh 70 kg or less:

There are 25 people who weigh 70 kg or less.
We can represent this as fun(weights, goal=70) = 25.

Step 2: Count all people weighing less than or equal to 69 kg
Now, let’s count all the people who weigh 69 kg or less. These are people who weigh:

Less than 70 kg (like 69 kg, 60 kg, 50 kg, etc.)
But not those who weigh exactly 70 kg.
Let’s say there are 18 people who weigh 69 kg or less.

We can represent this as fun(weights, goal=69) = 18.

Step 3: Subtract the two results
To find out how many people weigh exactly 70 kg, we subtract:

fun(weights, goal=70) (people weighing 70 kg or less) = 25
fun(weights, goal=69) (people weighing 69 kg or less) = 18
The number of people who weigh exactly 70 kg is:

25 - 18 = 7 people.
General Formula:
fun(weights, goal) counts how many people have a weight less than or equal to the goal (here, 70 kg).
fun(weights, goal-1) counts how many people have a weight less than or equal to goal - 1 (here, 69 kg).
By subtracting the two, you get the number of people who weigh exactly the goal weight.
Why it works:
This technique isolates the exact count of people (or items) at the goal value by subtracting the number of items below the goal from the number of items less than or equal to the goal. It's easier than directly counting "exact" matches in some problems, which is why this approach is useful.

If we replace while(sum > goal) with if(sum > goal), we would only shrink the window once per iteration, even if the sum is still greater than goal.

This can cause incorrect results because we may still have an invalid sum in the window when moving forward.

Example to Illustrate the Difference

nums = [2, 1, 3, 4], goal = 5
Using while (sum > goal) (Correct Approach)

l = 0, r = 0, sum = 2 → sum ≤ 5, valid
l = 0, r = 1, sum = 3 → sum ≤ 5, valid
l = 0, r = 2, sum = 6 → sum > 5, shrink `l` → sum = 4, valid
l = 1, r = 3, sum = 8 → sum > 5, shrink `l` → sum = 7, still > 5, shrink `l` again → sum = 4, valid
✅ We correctly shrink the window multiple times when needed.

Using if (sum > goal) (Incorrect Approach)

l = 0, r = 0, sum = 2 → sum ≤ 5, valid
l = 0, r = 1, sum = 3 → sum ≤ 5, valid
l = 0, r = 2, sum = 6 → sum > 5, shrink `l` once → sum = 4, valid
l = 1, r = 3, sum = 8 → sum > 5, shrink `l` *only once* → sum = 7, still > 5! ❌ Incorrect
❌ The window still has an invalid sum because we only shrank once instead of continuously.

here is my solution O(2N) using sliding window ,it is based on the concept that once you reach the sum at a given one take and shrink the window till it's limit after which the condition shall fail call this left 1,now in future if any 1 comes all the zeroes before left 1 are useless and thus arent needed just remove this one and shrink again till minimum valid window while increasing count
class Solution {
public:
int numberOfSubarrays(vector<int>& arr, int k) {
int ones = 0, l = 0, r = 0, count = 0, temp = 0;

while (r < arr.size()) {
if (arr[r] == 1)
ones++;

if (ones > k) {
while (ones > k) {
if (arr[l] == 1)
ones--;
l++;
}
temp = 0;
}

if (ones == k) {
temp = 0;
int t = l;
while (t < r && arr[t] == 0) {
temp++;
t++;
}
count += (temp + 1);
}

r++;
}

return count;
}
};

public String minWindow(String s, String t) {
int n = s.length(), m = t.length();
if(m > n) {
return "";
}

int left = 0, right = 0;
int minLength = Integer.MAX_VALUE, startIdx = -1;
int count = 0;

int[] chars = new int[256];
for(int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
chars[t.charAt(i)]++;
}

while(right < n) {
char c = s.charAt(right);
if(chars[c] > 0) {
count++;
}
chars[c]--;

while(count == m) {
int currentLength = right - left + 1;
if(currentLength < minLength) {
minLength = currentLength;
startIdx = left;
}
chars[s.charAt(left)]++;
if(chars[s.charAt(left)] > 0) {
count--;
}
left = left + 1;
}
right = right + 1;
}
return startIdx == -1 ? "" : s.substring(startIdx, startIdx + minLength);
}

class Solution

//Function to find minimum time required to rot all oranges.
int orangesRotting(vector<vector<int>>& grid) {
// Code here
vector<vector<int>> ans=grid;
int n=ans.size();
int m=ans[0].size();
queue<pair<pair<int,int>,int>> q;
for(int i=0;i<n;i++){
for(int j=0;j<m;j++){
if(ans[i][j]==2)
q.push({{i,j},0});
}
}
int cnt,mxcnt=0;
int row,col,nrow,ncol;
int delRow[]={-1,0,1,0};
int delCol[]={0,1,0,-1};
while(!q.empty()){
row=q.front().first.first;
col=q.front().first.second;
cnt=q.front().second;
mxcnt=max(mxcnt,cnt);
q.pop();
for(int i=0;i<4;i++){
nrow=row+delRow[i];
ncol=col+delCol[i];
if((nrow>=0 && nrow<n) && (ncol>=0 && ncol<m) && ans[nrow][ncol]==1){
ans[nrow][ncol]=2;
q.push({{nrow,ncol},cnt+1});
}
}
}
for(int i=0;i<n;i++){
for(int j=0;j<m;j++){
if(ans[i][j]==1)
return -1;
}
}
return mxcnt;
}
};

Here's the postorder morris traversal(similar to preorder), the only changes are instead of finding the rightmost node in the left subtree, we find the leftmost node in the right subtree. Also, we need to keep adding the node values in the head so as to maintain the LRN order of postorder.

public List<Integer> postorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
List<Integer> arr = new LinkedList<>();
TreeNode curr = root;

while(curr != null){
if(curr.right == null){
arr.add(0,curr.val);
curr = curr.left;
}
else{
TreeNode temp = curr.right;
while(temp.left != null && temp.left != curr)
temp = temp.left;
if(temp.left == null){
temp.left = curr;
arr.add(0,curr.val);
curr = curr.right;
}
else{
temp.left = null;
curr = curr.left;
}
}
}
return arr;
}

For post order Morris Traversal->
We will modify the preorder morris traversal from root->left->right to root->right->left. For this we need to do one more change. While in normal preorder and inorder, we were creating thread from right most node of left subtree to present node, here we will create thread from left most node of right subtree to present node as here we have to cover right subtree before left subtree

class Solution {
public:
vector<int> postorderTraversal(TreeNode* root) {
vector<int> ans;
while(root)
{
TreeNode *curr = root;//We will create thread from left most node of right subtree to present node and will
//travell to that node using curr
if(curr->right)//if root has right child
//We can't push directly this root node val to ans as we are not sure whether we are here
//thorough thread link after covering right subtree or we are here for the first time
{
curr = curr->right;
while(curr->left && curr->left != root)//go to left most node of right subtree
curr=curr->left;
if(curr->left != root)//not threaded yet
{
ans.push_back(root->val);//it means root was visited for first time and this is modified preorder hence
//push this node's val to ans
curr->left = root;//create the thread
root = root->right;//go to right to cover right subtree as modified preorder is root->right->left
}
else//was threaded
{
curr->left = NULL;//break the thread
root = root->left;//right subtree has been covered hence now cover the left one
//no need to push this node value as we are here for the second time using thread
//link
}
}
else//root hasn't right child
{
ans.push_back(root->val);//modified preorder is root->right->left hence push this value before going to left
root = root->left;
}
}
reverse(ans.begin(),ans.end());//reversing root->right->left to left->right->root to make it post order
return ans;
}
};

class Solution {
private:
bool isSafe(int source, vector<int> adj[], vector<int> &safe, vector<int> &vec) {
safe[source] = -1;
for(auto v:adj[source]) {
if(!safe[v]) {
if(isSafe(v, adj, safe, vec)) {
safe[v] = 1;
vec.push_back(v);
}
else return false;
}
else if(safe[v] == -1) return false;
}
return true;
}
public:
vector<int> eventualSafeNodes(int V, vector<int> adj[]) {
vector<int> vec;
vector<int> safe(V, 0);
for(int i = 0; i < V; i++)
if(!safe[i]) {
if(isSafe(i, adj, safe, vec)) {
safe[i] = 1;
vec.push_back(i);
}
}
sort(vec.begin(), vec.end());
return vec;
}
};

func singleNonDuplicate(_ arr: [Int]) -> Int {

if arr.count == 1 {

The other better approach without using DSU can be to use a set in which all the deadlines till the maxDeadLine + 1 will be inserted and we will find the lower bound of the current value. If the lower bound is equal to the given value, we will use that and remove from the set and if the lower bound is greater than the deadline we will find the just smaller iterator.
In other words, our set contains all those deadlines on which tasks are not performed and now by lower bound we are trying to find out the last index on which the task can be done. Using lower bound, it will give the time equal to or just greater than the deadline which is available for job. Now, if the time returned is greater we will move to the previous iterator to get the just smaller available time. And then if the value is available we will remove that time from the set because now this particular time is also not available for performing the task.

Code to the approach:

class Solution {
public:

vector<int> jobSequencing(vector<int> &deadline, vector<int> &profit) {
int n = deadline.size();
vector<pair<int,int>>vec(n);
int maxDeadLine = 0;
for(int i = 0;i < n;i++){
vec[i] = {profit[i],deadline[i]};
maxDeadLine = max(maxDeadLine,deadline[i]);
}
set<int>st;
for(int i = 0;i < maxDeadLine+2;i++){
st.insert(i);
}
sort(vec.begin(),vec.end());
int jobCnt = 0;
int sumProfit = 0;
for(int i = n-1;i >= 0;i--){
int endTime = vec[i].second;
auto it = st.lower_bound(endTime);
if(it!=st.end()){
int time = (*it);
if(time==endTime){
jobCnt++;
sumProfit += vec[i].first;
st.erase(it);
}else if(time>endTime){
it--;
int time = (*it);
if(time>0){
jobCnt++;
sumProfit += vec[i].first;
st.erase(it);
}
}
}
}
vector<int>ans = {jobCnt,sumProfit};
return ans;
}
};

class Solution {
public:
vector<int> jobSequencing(vector<int> &deadline, vector<int> &profit) {
// code here
int max_deadlines = *max_element(deadline.begin(), deadline.end());
int n = profit.size();

set<int> st;

for(int i = 1; i <= max_deadlines; i++) st.insert(i);

vector<pair<int,int>> vec;

for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
vec.push_back({profit[i], deadline[i]});
}

sort(vec.begin(), vec.end(), greater<pair<int,int>>());

int cnt = 0;
int max_profit = 0;

for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
int profit = vec[i].first;
int deadline = vec[i].second;

auto it = st.upper_bound(deadline);

if (it != st.begin()) {
--it;
st.erase(it);
cnt++;
max_profit += profit;
}
}

return {cnt, max_profit};
}
};

int characterReplacement(string s, int k) {
vector<int> count(26, 0);
int left = 0, maxFreq = 0, maxLen = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < s.size(); ++right) {
count[s[right] - 'A']++;
maxFreq = max(maxFreq, count[s[right] - 'A']);

int windowSize = right - left + 1;

// If more than k changes needed, shrink window
if (windowSize - maxFreq > k) {
count[s[left] - 'A']--;
left++;
}

maxLen = max(maxLen, right - left + 1);
}

return maxLen;
}

text_display: For people like me who struggle to understand why maxFreq is not updated: In the sliding window technique, when the window becomes invalid, we always shrink the window size to preserve the last valid answer. If we don't shrink, we risk updating maxLen or the answer using an invalid window. Keeping this in mind, if we were to decrease maxFreq, it would alter our calculation (len - maxFreq < K) and potentially lead to incorrect results. By leaving maxFreq unchanged and shrinking the window until it becomes valid again, we ensure that the last valid answer (maxLen) remains intact.

class Solution {
public:
int widthOfBinaryTree(TreeNode* root) {

if(!root) return 0;

queue<pair<TreeNode*,int>>q;
q.push({root,0});
int ans=0;
while(!q.empty())
{
int size=q.size();
int mn=q.front().second;
int first,last;

for(int i=0;i<size;i++)
{
int curr=q.front().second-mn;
TreeNode* node=q.front().first;
q.pop();
if(i==0) first=curr;
if(i==size-1) last=curr;
if(node->left)
q.push({node->left,(long long)curr*2+1});
if(node->right)
q.push({node->right,(long long)curr*2+2});
}
ans=max(ans,last-first+1);

}
return ans;

}
};

class Solution {
private class Pair{
int idx;

Pair(int idx, TreeNode node){
this.idx=idx;
this.node=node;
}
}
public int widthOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
Queue<Pair> q=new LinkedList<Pair>();
Pair temp;
int width=0, begin, end, size;
q.add(new Pair(0, root));

while(!q.isEmpty()){
size=q.size();
temp=q.poll();
begin=temp.idx;
end=temp.idx;

if(temp.node.left!=null){
q.add(new Pair(2*end, temp.node.left));
}
if(temp.node.right!=null){
q.add(new Pair((2*end)+1, temp.node.right));
}
for(int i=2;i<=size;i++){
temp=q.poll();
end=temp.idx;

if(temp.node.left!=null){
q.add(new Pair(2*end, temp.node.left));
}
if(temp.node.right!=null){
q.add(new Pair((2*end)+1, temp.node.right));
}
}
if(end-begin+1>width){
width=end-begin+1;
}
}
return width;
}
}

class Solution {
public:
int maxScore(vector<int>& cardPoints, int k) {
int n = cardPoints.size();
int left = n-k;
int right = n-k;
int ans = 0;
int sum = 0;
while (left < n) {

if ((right - left + 1) <= k) {

sum = sum + cardPoints[right % n];
right++;

} else {

sum = sum + cardPoints[right % n];
sum = sum - cardPoints[left++];
right++;
}
ans = max(sum, ans);
}
return ans;
}
};
